question.text: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2-y^2+xy+2x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,-1).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,-1)$, can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,-1).$

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} ( x^2-y^2+xy+2x+y ) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} ( x^2-y^2+xy+2x+y ) \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= (2x+y+2) \ \mathbf i + (-2y+x+1) \ \mathbf j\\[7pt] \nabla f(1,-1) &= (2(1) + (-1) + 2) \ \mathbf i + (-2(-1) + 1 + 1) \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= 3 \, \mathbf i + 4 \, \mathbf j \end{align}

Finally, we normalize $\nabla f(1,-1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\nabla f(1,-1)}{\| \nabla f(1,-1) \|} & = \dfrac{3 \, \mathbf i + 4 \, \mathbf j}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}} = \dfrac{1}{5}\left(3\,\mathbf i + 4\, \mathbf j\right) \end{align*}

question.text: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2-2xy+8y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (2,-2).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (2,-2)$, can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,-2).$

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (2,-2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (x^2+y^2-2xy+8y ) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (x^2+y^2-2xy+8y ) \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= (2x-2y) \ \mathbf i + (2y-2x+8) \ \mathbf j\\[7pt] \nabla f(2,-2) &= (2(2) - 2(-2)) \ \mathbf i + (2(-2) - 2(2) + 8) \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= 8 \, \mathbf i \end{align}

Finally, we normalize $\nabla f(2,-2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\nabla f(2,-2)}{\| \nabla f(2,-2) \|} & = \dfrac{8 \, \mathbf i}{\sqrt{8^2}} = \mathbf i \end{align*}

question.text: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = \sqrt{x} + 2\sqrt{y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 4).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y) = (1,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,4).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,4)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (\sqrt{x} + 2\sqrt{y}) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (\sqrt{x} + 2\sqrt{y}) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \, \mathbf j\\[7pt] \nabla f(1,4) &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{1}} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4}} \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{1}{2} \, \mathbf j\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left( \mathbf i + \mathbf j\right) \end{align*}

Finally, we normalize $\nabla f(1,4)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \dfrac{\nabla f(1,4)}{\| \nabla f(1,4) \|} & = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf i + \mathbf j)}{\left\| \dfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf i + \mathbf j )\right\|} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} \right)} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\left( \mathbf i + \mathbf j\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\mathbf i + \mathbf j)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf i + \mathbf j). \end{align}

question.text: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = \ln(x+y)-xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = \left(2, -1\right).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = \left(2,-1\right)$, can be found by computing $\nabla f\left(2,-1\right).$

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y) = \left(2,-1\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\ln(x+y)-xy\right) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\ln(x+y)-xy\right) \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{1}{x+y}-y\right) \ \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{1}{x+y}-x\right) \ \mathbf j\\[7pt] \nabla f\left(2,-1\right) &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2+(-1)}-(-1)\right) \ \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{1}{2+(-1)}-2\right) \ \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= 2\mathbf i - \mathbf j \end{align}

Finally, we normalize $\nabla f\left(2, -1\right)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\nabla f\left(2,-1\right)}{\| \nabla f\left(2,-1\right) \|} &= \dfrac{2\mathbf i - \mathbf j}{\sqrt{\left(2\right)^2+\left(-1\right)^2}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2\mathbf i - \mathbf j}{\sqrt{5}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(2\mathbf i - \mathbf j) \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the plane curve $2y - x = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2y}\right).$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align} 2y-x &= \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2y}\right) \\[5pt] \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2y}\right) - 2y + x & = 0 \end{align}

If we set $f(x,y) = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2y}\right) - 2y + x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2y}\right) - 2y + x\right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2y}\right) - 2y + x\right) \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{2y}{x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2y}+1\right) \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{2y}{x}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{x}{2y^2}\right)-2\right) \mathbf j\\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{1}{x}+1\right) \mathbf i + \left(-\dfrac{1}{y}-2\right) \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(2,1) &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right) \mathbf i + \left(-\dfrac{1}{1}-2\right) \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \, \mathbf i -3 \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \left\langle \dfrac{3}{2}, -3 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(3,1)= \left\langle \dfrac{3}{2}, -3 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x} &= \dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-2}{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)} &= \dfrac{y-1}{(-3)} \\[5pt] -3(x-2) &= \dfrac{3}{2}(y-1) \\[5pt] -6(x-2) &= 3(y-1) \\[5pt] -2(x-2) &= y-1 \\[5pt] -2x + 4 & = y - 1\\[5pt] 2x + y - 5 & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{y^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^2}{9} = 1.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,4).$
question.explanation:
If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^2}{9}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,4)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\dfrac{y^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^2}{9}\right) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\dfrac{y^2}{16}-\dfrac{x^2}{9}\right) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 2 9 x \, \mathbf i + \dfrac 1 8 y \, \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(0,4) &= -\dfrac 2 9(0)\, \mathbf i + \dfrac 1 8(4) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2 \, \mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 0, \dfrac 1 2 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \dfrac 1 2 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} (x-x_0)v_y - (y-y_0)v_x &= 0 \\[5pt] (x-0)\dfrac 1 2 - (y-4)0 &= 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac 1 2x &= 0 \\[5pt] x &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the plane curve $\sin(x^2y) = x^2-y^2-1.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align} \sin(x^2y) &= x^2-y^2-1 \\[5pt] \sin(x^2y) - x^2 + y^2 &= -1 \end{align}

If we set $f(x,y) = \sin(x^2y) - x^2 + y^2$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (\sin(x^2y) - x^2 + y^2) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (\sin(x^2y) - x^2 + y^2) \mathbf j \\[5pt] & = \left(2xy\cos(x^2y) - 2x\right) \mathbf i + \left(x^2\cos(x^2y) + 2y\right) \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(1,0) &= \left(2(1)(0)\cos((1^2)(0)) - 2(1)\right) \mathbf i + \left((1)^2\cos((1^2)(0)) + 2(0)\right) \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= -2\, \mathbf i + \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \langle -2, 1 \rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(1,0)= \langle -2, 1 \rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x} &= \dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-1}{-2} &= \dfrac{y-0}{1} \\[5pt] x-1 &= -2y \\[5pt] x+2y-1 &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the plane curve $\cos(xy) = x^2+y.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align} \cos(xy) &= x^2+y \\[3pt] \cos(xy) - x^2 - y &= 0 \end{align}

If we set $f(x,y) = \cos(xy) - x^2 - y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (\cos(xy) - x^2 - y) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (\cos(xy) - x^2 - y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \left(-y\sin(xy)-2x\right) \, \mathbf i + \left(-x\sin(xy)-1\right) \, \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(-1,0) &= \left(-0 \cdot \sin((-1) \cdot 0)-2 \cdot (-1)\right) \, \mathbf i + \left(-(-1) \cdot \sin((-1) \cdot 0)-1\right) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= 2\, \mathbf i - \mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \langle 2, -1 \rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(-1,0)= \langle 2, -1 \rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x} &= \dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-(-1)}{2} &= \dfrac{y-0}{-1} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x+1}{2} &= -y \\[5pt] x+1 &= -2y \\[5pt] x+2y+1&=0 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the plane curve $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=2y-x-2.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,2).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} &= 2y-x-2 \\[5pt] \sqrt{x^2+y^2}-2y+x &= -2 \end{align}

If we set $f(x,y) = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}-2y+x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,2)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( \sqrt{x^2+y^2}-2y+x\right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( \sqrt{x^2+y^2}-2y+x\right) \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}+1\right) \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}-2\right) \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(0,2) &= \left(\dfrac{0}{\sqrt{0^2+2^2}}+1\right) \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{0^2+2^2}}-2\right) \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \mathbf i - \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \langle 1, -1 \rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(0,2)= \langle 1, -1 \rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,2).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x} &= \dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-0}{1} &= \dfrac{y-2}{-1} \\[5pt] x &= 2-y \\[5pt] x+y &= 2 \end{align*}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (-1,0,1).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (-1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(-1,0,1).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (-1,0,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (x^2 + y^2 + z^2) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (x^2 + y^2 + z^2) \, \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (x^2 + y^2 + z^2) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = 2x\ \mathbf i + 2y \ \mathbf j + 2z \ \mathbf k\\[7pt] \nabla f(-1,0,1) & = 2(-1) \, \mathbf i + 2(0) \, \mathbf j + 2(1) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = -2 \, \mathbf i + 2 \, \mathbf k \end{align*}

Therefore, $-2 \, \mathbf i + 2\, \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (-1,0,1).$

question.text: For the function $f(x,y,z) = \ln(z^2-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (1,-2,0).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,-2,0).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (1,-2,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (\ln(z^2-xy)-yz) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (\ln(z^2-xy)-yz) \, \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (\ln(z^2-xy)-yz) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{y}{z^2-xy} \ \mathbf i + \left(-\dfrac{x}{z^2-xy}-z\right) \ \mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{2z}{z^2-xy}-y\right) \ \mathbf k\\[7pt] \nabla f(1,-2,0) & = -\dfrac{(-2)}{(0)^2-(1)(-2)} \, \mathbf i + \left(-\dfrac{1}{(0)^2-(1)(-2)}-0\right) \, \mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{2(0)}{(0)^2-(1)(-2)}-(-2)\right) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = \mathbf i - \dfrac 1 2\,\mathbf j + 2\,\mathbf k \end{align*}

Therefore, $\mathbf i - \dfrac 1 2 \,\mathbf j + 2\,\mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (1,-2,0).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(-2,-3,1).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (-2,-3,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (2x^2 + z^2 -xy) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (2x^2 + z^2 -xy) \, \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (2x^2 + z^2 -xy) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = (4x - y)\ \mathbf i - x \ \mathbf j + 2z \ \mathbf k\\[7pt] \nabla f(-2,-3,1) & = (4(-2) - (-3)) \, \mathbf i - (-2) \, \mathbf j + 2(1) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = -5 \, \mathbf i + 2\, \mathbf j + 2 \, \mathbf k \end{align*}

Therefore, $-5 \, \mathbf i + 2\,\mathbf j + 2 \, \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (-2,-3,1).$

question.text: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x^2+y^2+z^2 = 3$ at the point $(-1,-1,1).$
question.explanation:
If we set $f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(-1,-1,1).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^2+y^2+z^2 \right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( x^2+y^2+z^2\right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( x^2+y^2+z^2 \right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 2x \ \mathbf i + 2y \ \mathbf j + 2z \ \mathbf k \\[7pt] \nabla f(-1, -1, 1) &= 2(-1) \ \mathbf i + 2(-1) \ \mathbf j + 2(1) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= -2\, \mathbf i -2 \, \mathbf j + 2\,\mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle -2, -2, 2 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x - x_0}{v_x} = \dfrac{y - y_0}{v_y} = \dfrac{z - z_0}{v_z} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x - (-1)}{-2} = \dfrac{y - (-1)}{-2} = \dfrac{z - 1}{2} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x+1}{-2} = \dfrac{y +1}{-2} = \dfrac{z - 1}{2} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x+1}{1} = \dfrac{y+1}{1} = \dfrac{z-1}{-1} \\[5pt] x+1 = y+1 = \dfrac{z-1}{-1} \end{align*}

question.text: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\ln(x+y+z) = \ln(2) - xyz$ at the point $(1, 0, 1).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

\begin{align*} \ln(x+y+z) &= \ln(2)-xyz \\[5pt] \ln(x+y+z)+xyz &= \ln(2) \end{align*}

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\ln(2).$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,0,1).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( \ln(x+y+z)+xyz \right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( \ln(x+y+z)+xyz \right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( \ln(x+y+z)+xyz \right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{1}{x+y+z}+yz\right) \ \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{1}{x+y+z}+xz\right) \ \mathbf j + \left( \dfrac{1}{x+y+z}+xy\right) \ \mathbf k \\[7pt] \nabla f(1, 0, 1) &= \left(\dfrac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1)\right) \, \mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1)\right) \ \mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0)\right) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\,\mathbf i + \dfrac 3 2\,\mathbf j + \dfrac 1 2 \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \left\langle \dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 3 2, \dfrac 1 2 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} &= \langle 1, 0, 1 \rangle + t \, \nabla f(1,0,1) = \langle 1, 0, 1 \rangle + t \, \left\langle \dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 3 2, \dfrac 1 2 \right\rangle, \end{align*} where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

question.text: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $x^2 + \dfrac {y^2}9 + \dfrac {z^2}4 = 1$ at the point $(0, 0, 2).$
question.explanation:
First, note that we can write the equation of our surface as \begin{align*} x^2 + \dfrac {y^2}9 + \dfrac {z^2}4 - 1 =0 \end{align*}

So, if we set $f(x,y,z) =x^2 + \dfrac {y^2}9 + \dfrac {z^2}4 - 1 $, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,0,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x^2 + \dfrac {y^2}9 + \dfrac {z^2}4 -1\right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( x^2 + \dfrac {y^2}9 + \dfrac {z^2}4-1\right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(x^2 + \dfrac {y^2}9 + \dfrac {z^2}4-1\right) \mathbf k\\[3pt] &= 2 x \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {2y}9 \ \mathbf j + \dfrac z 2 \ \mathbf k\\[7pt] \nabla f(0, 0, 2) &= 2 (0) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {2(0)}9 \ \mathbf j + \dfrac {(2) }2 \ \mathbf k\\[3pt] &= \mathbf k\\[3pt] &= \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle \end{align}

Finally, the vector form of the equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,0,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be written as

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} &= \langle 0, \:0, \:2 \rangle + t \, \nabla f(0,0,2) = \langle 0, \: 0, \: 2 \rangle + t \, \langle 0, \: 0, \: 1 \rangle \end{align*} where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

question.text: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z^2\sin(x^2y) = x^2z+y - \dfrac{\pi}{2} $ at the point $\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align*} z^2\sin(x^2y) &= x^2z+y - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\\[5pt] z^2\sin(x^2y) - x^2z-y & = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{align*}

If we set $f(x,y,z) = z^2\sin(x^2y) -x^2z-y,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z) = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(z^2\sin(x^2y) -x^2z-y \right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(z^2\sin(x^2y) - x^2z-y\right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( z^2\sin(x^2y) - x^2z-y\right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = \left(2xyz^2\cos(x^2y) -2xz\right) \mathbf i + \left(x^2z^2\cos(x^2y) - 1 \right) \mathbf j + \left(2z\sin(x^2y) - x^2 \right) \mathbf k \\[7pt] \nabla f\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right) &= \left(2(-1)\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)(1)^2\cos{\left((-1)^2\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} -2(-1)(1)\right) \mathbf i + \left((-1)^2(1)^2\cos{\left((-1)^2\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} -1 \right) \mathbf j + \left(2(1)\sin{\left((-1)^2\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} -(-1)^2 \right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = \left(-\pi\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} +2\right) \mathbf i + \left(\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} -1 \right) \mathbf j + \left(2\sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} -1 \right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 2\,\mathbf i - \mathbf j + \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle 2, -1, 1 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$ and passes through the point $\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$ can be written as

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} &= \left\langle -1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1 \right\rangle + t \, \nabla f\left(-1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right) = \left\langle -1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1 \right\rangle + t \, \langle 2, -1, 1 \rangle, \end{align*} where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

question.text: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 = z^2$ at the point $(2, 0, 1).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 &= z^2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 - z^2 &= 0 \end{align*}

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 - z^2$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,0,1).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0,1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( \dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 - z^2 \right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( \dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 - z^2\right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( \dfrac{x^2}4 - y^2 - z^2\right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac x 2 \ \mathbf i - 2y \ \mathbf j - 2z \ \mathbf k \\[7pt] \nabla f(2, 0, 1) &= \dfrac{(2)}{2} \, \mathbf i - 2(0) \ \mathbf j - 2(1) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \mathbf i - 2 \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle 1, 0, -2 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be written as

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r} &= \langle 2, 0, 1 \rangle + t \, \nabla f(2,0,1) = \langle 2, 0, 1 \rangle + t \, \langle 1, 0, -2 \rangle, \end{align*} where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$
